title: If AI Is Cheating, What Do You Call It When Teachers Use It
author: Stephanie Holt
summary: Stephanie Holt argues that schools tell students AI is cheating while teachers use it to write worksheets and plan lessons, and that the contradiction persists because adults have not explained what separates appropriate from inappropriate use. She holds that policy, detection and bans cannot produce responsible use, and that the real question is what a student must contribute to the learning a task is designed to develop. Mixed messages across classrooms look arbitrary unless teachers share a language for explaining why boundaries differ by subject and task. She discusses cognitive offloading, asking what is being offloaded and whether doing so helps or hinders learning, and stresses metacognition. Her practical tool is a red, amber and green traffic light describing whether AI is appropriate for a particular purpose, with three self-questions about purpose, which thinking must remain mine, and how to check the result. She closes by arguing that culture change requires leaders to model transparency and trust teachers’ professional judgment.
points: The difference between a student submitting an AI essay as evidence of independent writing and a teacher drafting then checking a worksheet is about purpose, responsibility, transparency and the learning the task is meant to develop.
Policies do not create consistency; students experience school lesson by lesson, so teachers need a shared language to explain why AI rules differ across subjects.
A red, amber and green framework labels the appropriateness of AI for a purpose in context, not tools themselves, and three questions turn it into a decision aid.
Cognitive offloading is not automatically bad; the question is what is being offloaded and whether the offloaded work is the thinking the student needs to practise.
quotes: We tell students that using AI is cheating, ban it from their homework, warn them about the dangers of relying on it and then go back to our desks and use it to write worksheets, plan lessons, generate questions and save ourselves time.
The real challenge is not getting AI into schools. It is developing a shared understanding of what good use looks like, and why.
If we want responsible users of AI, we have to teach responsibility, not simply demand compliance.

I think one of the biggest challenges for schools is the assumption that a policy creates consistency. It does not. Students experience school through their individual lessons, and they will make sense of AI through what their teachers say and do.
These are not inconsistencies. They are different applications of the same underlying principle: the use of AI must be determined by what the student is supposed to learn.
The educational question is what we are choosing to offload, and whether doing so helps or hinders the learning we want to see.
The technology has not changed. The learning objective and the expectations have.
What am I trying to learn or achieve? Which parts of the thinking need to remain mine? How will I check that the use of AI has helped rather than undermined that purpose?
